title: Ukrainian literature is a European literature
author: Andrey Kurkov
text:
Essays

Ukrainian literature is a European literature

November 18, 2026

Andrey Kurkov

Themes: Culture, History, Ukraine, War

Ukrainian literature has taken to the global stage to tell the world a simple fact: Ukraine’s stories are European stories.

Edgar Degas, Ukrainian Dancers, c. 1899. The National Gallery renamed the work, long known as ‘Russian Dancers’, in 2022. Credit: mauritius images GmbH

As a child, I disliked geometry but adored geography. Geometry struck me as something flat and detached from life; geography, by contrast, appeared wonderfully multidimensional and unpredictable. Geography captured my imagination and inspired me to dream. Later, I realised that both subjects share the same root: ‘geo’ – the Earth, the ground upon which humanity dwells.
Over time, my attitude toward geometry shifted, and I even developed a favourite geometric shape: the triangle. Yet, what fascinated me most was the simple line – a line capable of dividing everything into two parts: left and right, or top and bottom. Back then, I didn’t fully grasp that there is always a line that separates ‘mine’ from ‘yours’, what I like from what I dislike, and what is right from what is wrong.
In this sense, a line serves as the foundation for any boundary – whether it defines the limits of a nation state or the edges of one’s personal space.
Human beings typically inhabit two worlds simultaneously: a small, intimate sphere of close personal connections, and a ‘larger’ world defined by the borders of one’s nation state. The map of my country, Ukraine, has long been etched into my mind. For the 35 years since the collapse of the Soviet Union, I have carried an image of this map with me. In happier times, my family and I travelled by car along nearly the entire length of Ukraine’s borders. I wanted to help my children grasp the scale and geographical contours of Ukraine at a time when their own geopolitical imagination was still taking shape.
In 2014, Russia annexed Crimea and seized part of the Donbas, yet the map of Ukraine in my mind – in my imagination – has not changed. It still retains the very same contours it acquired in 1991. That map will remain as it is in my thoughts for the rest of my life.
For years, I have envisioned the contours of Ukraine much like a vessel being filled with wine and, since 1991, the wine flowing into that vessel is ‘meaning’ – specifically, Ukrainian meaning. It has been filling up with Ukrainian culture which has gradually displaced the Soviet culture that once occupied it almost completely. It has been refilling with the Ukrainian language – a language that the Russian Empire had spent more than 300 years systematically driving out of Ukrainian territory. Ukraine has been filling up with its own historically rooted, individualistic mentality, once again displacing the Soviet and Russian collective mentality.
As the processes that make Ukraine truly Ukrainian seemed to be accelerating – and as the distinction between Ukrainian life, founded on democratic principles, and the Russian authoritarian system became ever more stark – Russia decided, as it has so often in the past, to prevent Ukraine from becoming Ukraine.
Putin decided that Ukrainians did not deserve a sovereign state. He resolved to bring Ukraine back into the fold of the Russian Empire and to plunge Ukrainians once more into the ‘Russian world’ – a realm where some 150 ethnic groups co-exist, all equally disenfranchised, voiceless and stripped of the right to self-determination.
This summer, the Ukrainian book industry was dealt a particularly heavy blow: for three months, Russian missiles and drones systematically destroyed the warehouses of publishing houses and printing facilities. More than 12 million newly printed books – 30 per cent of the typical annual output – were consumed by the fires caused by the explosions. While this was not the first blow to Ukraine’s publishing industry, it was the most devastating, forcing small-scale publishers to cease operations entirely.
Many Ukrainians were left wondering: are book warehouses and printing shops marked as priority targets on the Russian military’s bombing maps?
In all likelihood, no. Russia is simply attempting to destroy all warehouse facilities, operating on the hope that some might contain drones or other weaponry. Yet, one cannot entirely rule out the possibility that the destruction of the Ukrainian book industry is intentional.
From the start of the war, Ukrainians took particular pride in the fact that, despite Russian terror, book print-runs and sales in Ukraine had actually increased, and dozens of new bookstores had opened. In this context, the destruction of book warehouses and printing facilities serves as a clear blow to public morale. In fact, as I write these words, Russia has launched another missile strike on Kyiv, severely damaging the building of the State Book Chamber – which houses a collection of every book ever published in Ukraine. This would be the equivalent of a missile strike on the British Library in London.
Until recently, Ukrainians took pride in the fact that, despite the war, trains in Ukraine continued to depart and arrive on schedule. Foreign correspondents in Kyiv wrote about it with astonishment, and European documentary filmmakers made films on the subject. However, over the past two months, Ukraine’s railway system has become a primary target.
In just the last few months, hundreds of passenger trains have been attacked by drones, and more than 500 locomotives have been destroyed or severely damaged. Recently, a drone exploded near the Polish border, close to a train carrying a European Union delegation returning from Kyiv – a train that was also transporting Boris Johnson. And yes, our trains no longer depart or arrive according to schedule.
I mention this because Ukraine’s railway system has a function parallel to that of our literary life and book industry. Both are vital means of socio-cultural transportation. Both provide for individual development and enrichment, and that is why they are both targeted so aggressively by Russia.
I have no doubt that Russia’s aggression against Ukraine envisages not only the seizure of all Ukrainian territory but also the destruction of Ukrainian culture – the obliteration of a Ukrainian cultural space that, in the years immediately preceding the war, had become highly visible on the global cultural map.
Culture – as an instrument of communication between peoples – tends to transcend geographical borders, becoming universal and supranational. Culture can and should facilitate communication and build bridges between nations; it can take on the role of a universal language which allows a people to explain their own history – and, conversely, to understand the history of others. Through this communication we gain supporters abroad who go on to act as cultural ambassadors or promoters of a culture that is not their own.
Of course, culture can also be tasked with the opposite objective: a weapon used to dismantle and suppress a neighbouring culture and take its place. Once an indigenous culture has been supplanted by that of the conquerors, they demand that the seized cultural space be recognised as their own physical territory.
This is already happening in the occupied territories of Ukraine. It is a repetition of what occurred in 1783, when the Russian Empire seized Crimea; subsequently, Russian culture suppressed the cultures of the Crimean Tatars, Krymchaks, and Karaites – the indigenous peoples of the peninsula.
Even today, Russia is not inventing anything new. It is drawing upon its own past – specifically, its historical experience of imperial expansion and the propagation of imperial Russian culture.
It is no coincidence that the City Drama Theatre in Mariupol – which was bombed and became a mass grave for many of the city’s residents – was, during renovation work, enclosed by high fences adorned with portraits of Pushkin, Tolstoy and Dostoevsky.
Over the past four and a half years, Ukraine has lost approximately 300 writers, poets and translators, as well as more than a thousand cultural figures – including those who worked in film, music and the visual arts. All of them were either killed at the front or fell victim to Russian missile and drone strikes.
The young writer Victoria Amelina died from severe injuries sustained when a Russian missile struck a pizzeria in the city of Kramatorsk. Early in the war, in the Kharkiv region, the children’s poet and author Volodymyr Vakulenko was shot and killed while his village was under occupation. The poet-soldier Borys Humeniuk went missing in action at the front.
Most of the 300 authors and translators so far lost during this war were young and in their creative prime – ready to further the development of Ukrainian literature. One can only guess at the number of unwritten or unfinished books that might have enriched Ukrainian literature, but which have, instead, become part of its ‘phantom corpus’.
The body of phantom literature – books that were conceived but never penned or published – is one of the reasons why Ukrainian literature remained largely unnoticed by the rest of the world for so long.
In the 1920s and 1930s, Ukrainian literature experienced an unprecedented flourishing. Ukrainian poetic futurism captivated the young; a new urban prose began to displace traditional novels centred on rural life; and the first adventure novels infused a sense of romance into an era that was already inherently revolutionary and romantic.
However, all this came to an abrupt end when a directive arrived from Moscow: an instruction to ‘restore order in Ukrainian literature and put an end to literary experimentation once and for all’. Restoring order meant the arrest of hundreds of Ukrainian intellectuals – writers, playwrights, theatre directors, and poets. These arrests were followed by mass executions, most of which took place in 1937 – the bloodiest year of the Soviet repressions.
Of the 300 Ukrainian writers who were actively working in 1930, only 36 remained by 1938. Out of the entire vibrant generation, only seven writers died of natural causes.
This cohort of Ukrainian writers has come to be known as the ‘Executed Renaissance’ (or ‘The Gunned Down Generation’). Looking at what these writers managed to produce and publish before the repressions, one can grasp the extent of the literature Ukraine lost when these authors were persecuted and killed.
Today, history is repeating itself. It is no longer the Soviet repressive apparatus that is seeking to destroy Ukrainian literature; rather, it is the Russian army and Russian agencies of political control that have imposed a rigid grip on the occupied territories and the Ukrainian citizens who remain there.
While many writers and poets are currently in military uniform, fighting on the front lines, the Russian authorities are purging their books from public libraries in the occupied territories, actively replacing Ukrainian works with Russian ones.
As early as 2023, Vladimir Medinsky – an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin – boasted that Russia had brought approximately 2.5 million books into the occupied territories. If one includes school textbooks printed specifically for these areas, that figure rises to 7.5 million. And this for a population of up to three million.
Although it is nearly impossible to fight a war and write simultaneously, Ukrainian writer-soldiers find themselves with no other choice but to try to do this, and we see books written (during the war) by soldiers being published and read back on the home front.
After several works of non-fiction, soldier-author Artem Chapeye has released a new novel, T-Shchastia (T-Happiness). T-Shchastia is a post-apocalyptic novel in which the protagonist, Viktor – a veteran of the Russo-Ukrainian War – finds himself completely alone in a territory occupied by the Russian victors. Behind him lies a happy prewar life and a family that now exists only in his memories. In this new reality, he faces profound isolation and a harsh, joyless existence, where his only solace is a device that creates an illusion of happiness. Viktor limits his use of this high-tech device to one hour a day, spending the remaining 23 hours navigating a tense and dangerous reality.
Artur Dron, a 25-year-old veteran of the Russo-Ukrainian War who was demobilised after sustaining severe injuries, has seen his autobiographical book, Hemingway Knows Nothing, published simultaneously in several countries. Hemingway Knows Nothing is a collection of autobiographical essays about war, infused with a soldier’s personal experiences, emotions, reflections, doubts, and pain. Through these texts, the author challenges the romanticisation of war.
Poet Yaryna Chornohuz – who serves in a drone battalion – has published a new collection of her poetry in Ukraine, the United States and France. She also writes poetry only about war and its impact on everybody and everything.
This war is also unique for Ukrainian literature in that soldier-writers and soldier-poets – sometimes in military uniform, sometimes not – regularly travel abroad to present their new books.
For nearly the entire month of October, Yaryna Chornohuz toured the United States to present her new book. Artem Chapeye presented his books in Finland and Sweden, while Artur Dron recently presented his work in Ireland and the United Kingdom.
Ukrainian media often report that citizens in Europe and the United States have grown weary of the war in Ukraine. While this is partly true, it is also true that people in Europe, the US, Japan and many other countries have not grown tired of Ukrainian literature – a body of work that has only come to the attention of international readers because of the war, and only within the last four and a half years.
During meetings with readers abroad, I am frequently asked whether contemporary Ukrainian writers produce books that are not about the war. This is, in fact, a very important question. Today, foreign audiences firmly associate Ukraine with war and its status as a victim of Russian aggression – a reality reflected in the majority of books by Ukrainian authors. Yet, among recent publications, there are works dedicated to another equally significant theme: the theme of memory.
Two novels have recently appeared in translation – Amadoka by Sofia Andrukhovych and Zabuttia (Forgottenness) by Tetiana Malyarchuk – in which memory itself acts as the central character.
War and memory – including the memory of war, and of all wars – are inseparable concepts. While war is invariably a historical tragedy, memory serves as the primary instrument through which any nation determines the proper place for a war within its own national history.
Both of the aforementioned novels take place across two time periods: the present and the past. Each attempts to interpret the history of Ukraine from the vantage point of today.
Amadoka explores, among other things, the Holocaust (in Ukraine) and the events that unfolded in Western Ukraine during the Second World War.
Forgottenness recounts the failed attempt to preserve Ukrainian independence during the Civil War of 1918-21 and how a short-lived reality once more became an unachievable dream.
These novels are valuable additions to the body of post-independence literature that offers Ukrainian readers opportunities to re-assess our history, but these novels have also successfully transcended the Ukrainian literary sphere to reach a European audience, as they tell universal human stories – tales of love, death, hope and disappointment – themes that lie at the heart of world literature.
While the context is distinctly Ukrainian – meaning that these stories carry a deeper resonance for Ukrainians than they might for international readers – the fact that these books are being read abroad is profoundly significant for Ukraine. They transport the reader right inside our country and its history, going beyond merely offering a window into a foreign culture.
At a time when Ukrainian books are being physically destroyed by Russian drones and missiles, the publication and reading of these works abroad suggests that translation serves as a vital act of preservation. By moving a text from its original language into another, a ‘back-up’ version is created – a safeguard against the potential destruction of the original. In this sense, the translation of Ukrainian literature facilitates ‘the migration’ of its finest works into a ‘cloud’ that can be seen the world over – a secure space for a literature that is currently threatened with annihilation.
Of course, memory encompasses far more than just the memory of war; it is a much broader, all-encompassing concept. A nation’s memory is proof of its very existence – and culture is the essential tool for shaping and sustaining that memory.
Because of the war, some Ukrainian classics, as well as contemporary works, have been translated and published abroad. These ‘standards’ of Ukrainian literature were previously entirely unknown in Europe and the United States. At last, for example, books by 19th- and 20th-century Ukrainian writers – such as Ivan Franko, Lesya Ukrainka, Olha Kobylianska and others – are becoming available in translation into foreign languages.
Nevertheless, the history of cultural relations between Ukraine – and Ukrainians – and Western Europe remains largely unknown. These chapters of history still require further research and broader dissemination.
Few people, even within Ukraine, are aware that the first book written by a Ukrainian author was composed in Latin in the Italian city of Bologna and published in Rome in February 1483. Its author, Yuriy Donat-Kotermak, was a professor at the University of Bologna at the time, having served as its rector in 1481-82. In Italy, he was known as Giorgio da Leopoli – ‘Giorgio from Lviv’.
Another prominent Ukrainian thinker, theologian, and author of polemical essays, Meletiy Smotrytsky, wrote in Polish and played a significant role in the intellectual life of Central Europe. During the same period, dozens of Ukrainian intellectuals took an active part in European debates concerning the role of religion in society, the influence of the Vatican and the conflict between Catholicism and Orthodoxy. These same intellectuals introduced Ukraine to Western and Central Europe, explaining its history, as well as its hopes and dreams.
Remarkably, this took place even amid ongoing military conflict; throughout the 16th and 17th centuries, Ukraine was in a state of constant war with both Russia and Poland. Today, amid a new war with Russia, Poland remains one of Ukraine’s primary allies; yet, historical grievances and resentments have not been forgotten – they are being exploited by far-right Polish politicians in the lead-up to the presidential election in 2027. In this context – that of Polish-Ukrainian relations – Ukrainian literature can play a vital role as a peacemaker and an advocate.
Even before the annexation of Crimea and the Euromaidan protests, Poland began to engage actively with Ukrainian literature – to such an extent that sales of works by Yurii Andrukhovych, one of the most significant contemporary Ukrainian authors, actually surpassed sales within Ukraine itself.
Ukrainian literature found a vast readership in Poland, and this surely contributed to Poland’s readiness to support Ukraine in 2022, at the very onset of the full-scale Russian aggression.
Sometimes, I feel that we underestimate the role and potential of literature. It is only now becoming clear that, in times of war, literature serves as a crucial component of both diplomacy and public education. It acts as a catalyst for decision-making – on both a personal and a political level.
Because of the war, Ukrainian literature – once known for its poetic, unhurried quality – has become dynamic, assertive, even militant. This is precisely why it has so rapidly penetrated European and other international book markets. It did not merely become a cry for help – though, at the start of the war, Ukrainian writers did indeed appeal to international readers for humanitarian aid for Ukraine. More than this, Ukrainian literature has become a record – a body of evidence documenting war crimes – while simultaneously serving as a practical manual for survival in wartime.
Victoria Amelina, who was killed when a Russian missile struck Kramatorsk, through her writing continues to tell readers in Brazil and France about the war in Ukraine, and about what this conflict means in the lives of Ukrainian women. Kateryna Yehorushkina, who remained in Kyiv under bombardment, explores in her documentary books – based on the stories of real people, both adults and children – how the meaning of the word ‘home’ shifts during wartime.
Writer and soldier Ostap Slyvynsky, in his book A Ukrainian Dictionary of War, shows readers around the world how war transforms language itself – its vocabulary, and even the meanings of long-familiar words.
Ukrainian literature has entered the global stage not to entertain readers or to dazzle them with geographical, folkloric, or social exotica. Rather, it has come to tell the world about the simple fact of Ukraine’s existence and that of its people – and it does so with every ounce of energy at its disposal.
My primary hope is that, in the aftermath of the war, Ukrainian literature will help ensure that Ukraine is not perceived by foreign readers solely through the lens of war or as a victim of aggression. Ukraine is part of Europe, and the stories told by Ukrainian writers are, in fact, European stories.
Ukrainian literature does belong to the European cultural sphere – a point that brings me back to my thoughts on geometry and geography. If you read a Ukrainian love story and find that it resonates with you, it serves as further proof that we inhabit the same cultural space, sharing the same values and ways of responding to the world around us. While Russia’s military has obliterated Ukraine’s state borders in the east, the border in the west – the one shared with the European Union – has become far more porous, facilitating the movement not only of refugees fleeing Ukraine but also of Ukrainian culture itself.
The cultural divide between Western Europe and Ukraine has ceased to exist. The absence of such a boundary is of vital importance to the future of the Ukrainian state. Supporting Ukraine’s European future is simple: read more books by Ukrainian authors, watch Ukrainian films, listen to Ukrainian music, and, in general, take a greater interest in Ukrainian culture.
The Lancaster International Fiction Lecture 2026 was given by Andrey Kurkov in the Faraday Lecture Theatre at Lancaster University on 12 November. The lecture, a collaboration between the School of Global Affairs at Lancaster University and Litfest (Lancaster Literature Festival), can be viewed via the Litfest website. Andrey Kurkov’s ‘Three Years on Fire: The Destruction of Ukraine’ is published by Open Borders Press and can be ordered online.

Author
Andrey Kurkov

Andrey Kurkov is a Ukrainian author, journalist and screenwriter. His novels include ‘Death and the Penguin’, ‘The Bickford Fuse’ and ‘Grey Bees’. His non-fiction works on the Russian invasion of Ukraine include ‘Our Daily War’ and ‘Three Years on Fire’. He was President of PEN Ukraine from 2018 to 2022 and lives in Kyiv.
